key_cases.holding: The statutory sunset date does not automatically divest a juvenile court of jurisdiction, but where the problems that gave rise to the original complaint have been resolved or sufficiently mitigated the court may not enter further dispositional orders on that complaint.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading Ohio authority requiring closure when the original basis for the case no longer exists.
key_cases.quote: Where the original problems have been resolved or sufficiently mitigated, courts may not make further dispositional orders based on the original complaint.

key_cases.holding: An order continuing temporary custody is not a final, appealable order, because although a juvenile custody hearing is a special proceeding the order must also affect a substantial right, and the continuation of temporary custody does not foreclose appropriate relief later.
key_cases.relevance: It distinguishes an order that ends the case from one that merely continues it, which controls when a dismissal or closure becomes reviewable.
key_cases.quote: While a juvenile custody hearing is a special proceeding, a juvenile court order must also affect a substantial right to be a final, appealable order under R.C. 2505.02(B)(2).

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of Ohio, First Appellate District
key_cases.holding: Affirming in part and reversing in part custody dispositions for four siblings, the court held that where reunification within a reasonable time was not possible the mandatory disposition of R.C. 2151.414(D)(2) applied, and it explained that sufficiency review asks whether the evidence justified the juvenile court's findings under the clear-and-convincing standard.
key_cases.relevance: It shows when an appellate court will set aside a disposition and return custody rather than let the case close on the agency's terms.
key_cases.quote: Our sufficiency review asks whether enough evidence exists to justify the juvenile court's relevant findings under a clear-and-convincing standard.

key_cases.holding: An adjudication of abuse, dependency or neglect coupled with an award of temporary custody under R.C. 2151.353(A)(2) is a final order that must be appealed within 30 days under App.R. 4(A), and App.R. 4(B)(5) gives no second opportunity to appeal that adjudication after the final dispositional order terminating parental rights.
key_cases.relevance: It distinguishes the orders that end the controversy when entered from those that leave issues pending, which controls when an adjudication or closure becomes reviewable.
key_cases.quote: App.R. 4(B)(5) does not apply to adjudication orders that include a finding of neglect, abuse, or dependency and a grant of temporary custody to a children services agency
